1. Read the requirement yaml. Note the JIRA id and the module it belongs to (HDFS / YARN / MAPREDUCE / HADOOP-common / tools).

225	    It is desirable for correctness of the system that only one NameNode be in
226	    the Active state at any given time. **Importantly, when using the Quorum
227	    Journal Manager, only one NameNode will ever be allowed to write to the
228	    JournalNodes, so there is no potential for corrupting the file system metadata
229	    from a split-brain scenario.** However, when a failover occurs, it is still
230	    possible that the previous Active NameNode could serve read requests to
231	    clients, which may be out of date until that NameNode shuts down when trying to
232	    write to the JournalNodes. For this reason, it is still desirable to configure
233	    some fencing methods even when using the Quorum Journal Manager. However, to
234	    improve the availability of the system in the event the fencing mechanisms
235	    fail, it is advisable to configure a fencing method which is guaranteed to
236	    return success as the last fencing method in the list. Note that if you choose
237	    to use no actual fencing methods, you still must configure something for this
238	    setting, for example "`shell(/bin/true)`".
239	
240	    The fencing methods used during a failover are configured as a
241	    carriage-return-separated list, which will be attempted in order until
242	    one indicates that fencing has succeeded. There are two methods which ship with
243	    Hadoop: *shell* and *sshfence*. For information on implementing your own custom
244	    fencing method, see the *org.apache.hadoop.ha.NodeFencer* class.
245	
246	    - - -
247	
248	    **sshfence** - SSH to the Active NameNode and kill the process
249	
250	    The *sshfence* option SSHes to the target node and uses *fuser* to kill the
251	    process listening on the service's TCP port. In order for this fencing option
252	    to work, it must be able to SSH to the target node without providing a
253	    passphrase. Thus, one must also configure the
254	    **dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.private-key-files** option, which is a
255	    comma-separated list of SSH private key files. For example:
256	
257	            <property>
258	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
259	              <value>sshfence</value>
260	            </property>
261	
262	            <property>
263	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.private-key-files</name>
264	              <value>/home/exampleuser/.ssh/id_rsa</value>
265	            </property>
266	
267	    Optionally, one may configure a non-standard username or port to perform the
268	    SSH. One may also configure a timeout, in milliseconds, for the SSH, after
269	    which this fencing method will be considered to have failed. It may be
270	    configured like so:
271	
272	            <property>
273	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
274	              <value>sshfence([[username][:port]])</value>
275	            </property>
276	            <property>
277	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.connect-timeout</name>
278	              <value>30000</value>
279	            </property>
280

283	    **shell** - run an arbitrary shell command to fence the Active NameNode
284	
285	    The *shell* fencing method runs an arbitrary shell command. It may be
286	    configured like so:
287	
288	            <property>
289	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
290	              <value>shell(/path/to/my/script.sh arg1 arg2 ...)</value>
291	            </property>
292	
293	    The string between '(' and ')' is passed directly to a bash shell and may not

295

297	    current Hadoop configuration variables, with the '\_' character replacing any
